title: Facilitate meaningful mathematical discourse
subtitle: Build shared understanding by getting students to compare, question, and connect each other’s mathematical ideas — not just report answers to you.

sections.sources: Source: NCTM, Principles to Actions (2014) · Smith & Stein, 5 Practices (2011) · Adding It Up (2001).

blocks.text: Effective teaching facilitates discourse among students to build a shared understanding of mathematical ideas by analyzing and comparing student approaches and arguments.

Discourse is not “more talking.” It is a purposeful exchange where student ideas are the material the class reasons about. The teacher’s job shifts from being the source of answers to **orchestrating a conversation** that adds up to the mathematics — deciding whose thinking to surface, in what order, and how to connect it. The alternative, teacher → student ping-pong through the same three hands, looks like participation but isn’t.
What it looks like in grades 6–8

items: Students talking *to each other* about mathematics, agreeing and disagreeing with reasons.
The teacher deliberately sequencing whose strategy is shared, and why.
Norms that make it safe to share unfinished thinking and to be wrong out loud.
A discussion that goes somewhere — it lands on a mathematical point, not just a parade of methods.

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: “I agree with ___ because…” / “Can I add on?”
Students revoicing and building on peers
The teacher purposefully choosing the order of ideas

no.title: We should *not* see
items: “Good job!” ending each answer (evaluation, not discourse)
A show-and-tell of random strategies with no thread
The same few voices carrying the room

blocks.text: Where it lives in our toolbelt

This is the payoff of [Talk Moves](/math/approach/talk-moves) — the moment-to-moment glue — and the goal of every opener: [Number Talks](/math/approach/number-talks), [Same But Different / WODB](/math/approach/same-but-different), and [Error Analysis](/math/approach/error-analysis). The [5 Practices](/math/approach/five-practices) are how you plan for it in a task.
Stop evaluating each answer. Instead of “yes, good,” ask “who can add on?” or “do you agree?” — and let the class do the reasoning. That one habit turns reporting into discourse.
